newsitem.title: USA: INSTANT VIEW -- U.S. April payrolls rise 142,000.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW -- U.S. April payrolls rise 142,000.

text.p: Following are comments from U.S. economists after the Labor Department reported the economy added 142,000 new jobs in April and the jobless rate fell to 4.9 percent, its lowest level in over 23 years. Jobs growth in March was revised downward to show a 139,000 increase compared to 175,000 originally.
Economists had expected 211,000 new jobs in the month and the unemployment rate to remain unchanged at 5.2 percent.
DAVID BLITZER, CHIEF ECONOMIST, STANDARD AND POOR'S: "This is a report with something for everyone.

"Wall Steet will probably love the average hourly earnings ... and the payrolls ... The politicians will be enamored with the 4.9 percent jobless rate ... Overall, the economy is doing very well," but Blitzer said some inflationary pressures may be percolating in the background.
Blitzer was speaking on Reuters Financial Television.
DAN SETO, SENIOR ECONOMIST, THE NIKKO SECURITIES CO INTERNATIONAL INC: "It looks like we had some weather problems involved here ... The most shocking element is the 4.9 percent unemployment rate.

Seto continued: "The decline in average hourly earnings should enable the (Treasury) market to hold at these levels. The numbers here suggest that, aside from weather-related problems, the economy is still very strong and the labor markets are very tight."

DAVID WYSS, RESEARCH DIRECTOR, DRI/MCGRAW HILL: "Very strong. The unemployment drop below 5.0 percent was probably the key here. That's a little scary. We haven't been below 5.0 percent since the early 1970s.

Wyss continued: "What it means is the economy still looks a lot stronger than it ought to. Now we did see a slowdown in the payroll number to a more sustainable pace -- 142,000 following 139,000, which is downwardly revised.
"We now have two months of moderate growth in payrolls, but that drop in the unemployment rate under 5.0 percent has to be scary to the (Federal Reserve," he added.
JOSEPH LIRO, CHIEF ECONOMIST, CIBC WOOD GUNDY SECURITIES CORP: "A real mixed bag.

"We had a downward revision to March an upward revision to February and a below-expected April, although a lot of that was due to the construction industry and a little bit to the manufacturing industry.

"The service sector was less affected by the weather and strikes and was up very strongly. To me the big negative was the drop in the unemployment rate. (The reason) was a drop in the labor force, which had been growing very, very strongly.
"To me the drop in the unemployment rate is very telling in terms of the prospects for Fed policy," Liro added.
"If you had to pick out one specific number (that would get the Fed's attention) it would be the jobless rate.
"The first month of the quarter tends to be the softest month for earnings anyhow. It's really a mixed bag, but I think the unemployment rate is the most decisive of the measures," he said.

ASTRID ADOLFSON, FIRST VICE PRESIDENT AND ECONOMIST, MCM MONEYWATCH INC: "The bottom line is that some of the weak components were really distorted probably because of the bad weather; you can see that in the construction jobs.

"But the very fact that the unemployment rate dropped so sharply -- well under 5.0 (percent) and the lowest level since 1973 -- let us say that the underlying tone in the labor market is still strong.
"This number still leaves open the door (for another Fed tightening in May)."
(( -- N.A. Treasury Desk, 212-859-1660 ))
